name: Morgan-Morgan Discs
description: Static thin discs of dust in Weyl's class, found by Thomas Morgan and Lesley Morgan in 1969. Half the dust circles the axis one way and half the other, so a disc has no angular momentum, and the field around it is a static vacuum built on a Newtonian potential.
convention: The mass parameter $m = GM/c^2$ is a length. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Spin a thin disc of dust fast enough and it does not fall in on itself: each grain circles the centre, held on its orbit by the pull of all the others [hunter1963]. What does general relativity make of such a disc? A spinning disc drags the inertial frames round with it, and a disc with no net angular momentum does not [bicak1993b]. So send half the dust round one way and half the other: each grain still circles the centre, the two streams pass through one another, and the spacetime is static [bicak1993b, lyndenbell1978].¶Thomas Morgan and Lesley Morgan, at the University of Nebraska, took up that disc in 1969 and gave the general solution of the static field equations for a disc of what they called "counterrotating" dust particles [morgan1969]. A spherical cluster held up the same way, by particles on circular orbits in every direction, was Albert Einstein's model of 1939, which they cite [einstein1939, morgan1969]. For a static vacuum field with an axis of symmetry, Hermann Weyl's reduction of 1917 leaves two functions of his coordinates $\rho$ and $z$: a potential $\psi$ that solves Laplace's equation of flat space, and a second function $\gamma$ found from $\psi$ by an integral [weyl1917, lehmkuhl2019]. Morgan and Morgan used the fact that for a thin disc Weyl's equation for $\psi$ is still Laplace's equation outside the disc, which makes finding $\psi$, as Donald Lynden-Bell and S. Pineault put it, "the classical problem of determining the potential of a given matter distribution in flat space" [lyndenbell1978]. The speed $V$ of each stream follows from the balance of gravity and centrifugal force on a grain, $\rho\,\partial_\rho\psi = V^2/(c^2 + V^2)$ [lyndenbell1978, bicak1993b].¶Which discs? C. Hunter had built Newtonian discs in 1963 in oblate spheroidal coordinates, in which a disc is a coordinate surface, by adding up elementary solutions of Laplace's equation [hunter1963, bardeen1969]. Morgan and Morgan's first family has a surface density proportional to a power of $1 - \rho^2$, with the radius of the disc as the unit of length [morgan1969]. In the notation of later papers the disc of order $n$, of mass $M$ and radius $a$, has the Newtonian density $(2n + 1)M(1 - \rho^2/a^2)^{n - 1/2}/2\pi a^2$ [semerak2002, gonzalez2006]. In Newton's theory the first of them turns uniformly, a disc that Hunter called "well-known" and that is now named the Kalnajs disc, after Agris Kalnajs's stellar discs of 1972 [hunter1963, kalnajs1972, gonzalez2006]. No grain may outrun light, and across this family that caps the redshift of light from the centre at $z = 1.5803$ [morgan1969].¶Their second family turns uniformly, $v^2 = \rho^2\omega^2e^{-4\phi}$ in their notation, with $\phi$ their potential and $\omega$ a constant [morgan1969]. James Bardeen had pointed out that these discs can have arbitrarily large redshifts without breaking the speed limit, and Morgan and Morgan showed that the redshift cannot pass $1.9015$ before the binding energy turns negative [morgan1969]. They concluded that the largest gravitational redshift of a counterrotating dust disc is "of order of magnitude 1" [morgan1969]. Later in 1969 Bardeen and Robert Wagoner computed the disc that turns one way only and set the two side by side: Morgan and Morgan's disc "is the same as ours in the Newtonian limit", and its binding energy peaks at about 5 percent of the rest mass energy [bardeen1969]. The binding energy of their own disc keeps growing with the redshift, which they tied to the dragging of inertial frames [bardeen1971]. An exact solution for the disc turning one way came in 1995 from Gernot Neugebauer and Reinhard Meinel [neugebauer1995].¶To Lynden-Bell and Pineault, writing in 1978, these were "rather odd solutions", whose advantage was "their simplicity which allows even finite disks to be solved exactly" and whose great disadvantage was "their artificiality" [lyndenbell1978]. By 1993 Jiří Bičák, Lynden-Bell, and Joseph Katz had shown that most vacuum Weyl solutions arise as the metrics of counterrotating discs, among them those of Curzon, Schwarzschild, and Zipoy and Voorhees [bicak1993]. The same year José Lemos and Patricio Letelier set a disc of Morgan and Morgan's family round a Schwarzschild black hole, an exact solution with three parameters: the mass of the hole, and the mass and the radius of the disc [lemos1993]. Christian Klein's stationary counterrotating dust discs of 2001 contain as limiting cases the static solutions of Morgan and Morgan and Neugebauer and Meinel's disc with one stream of matter [klein2001].¶William Bonnor and A. Sackfield had read one of Zipoy's spheroidal vacuum fields as the field of a disc in 1968, a year before Morgan and Morgan, and its density is infinite at the edge [bonnor1968]. The first Morgan-Morgan disc has a density that is finite everywhere, and was, in Oldřich Semerák's words, "referred to as the simplest physically acceptable one" [semerak2001]. Semerák found in 2001 that it has a curvature singularity at the rim all the same [semerak2001]. The higher members of the family are regular [semerak2001]. David Kofroň, Petr Kotlařík, and Semerák wrote Weyl's second function for the first discs in closed form in 2023, a polynomial in the spheroidal coordinates and in the arc cotangent of one of them [kofron2023].

related.text: The disc shrunk to a point. In the limit $a \to 0$ at fixed mass the potential of the disc is that of a point, $\psi = -m/R$, and Bičák, Lynden-Bell, and Katz showed that Curzon and Chazy's field itself arises as the metric of a counterrotating disc [bicak1993].
Einstein's sphere of particles on circular orbits in every direction. The disc is held up the same way within one plane, and Morgan and Morgan cite Einstein's paper [einstein1939, morgan1969].
A Weyl field as well, built on the Newtonian potential of a rod. Lemos and Letelier set a disc of this family round Schwarzschild's black hole, an exact solution of the two together [lemos1993].
Another static Weyl field, that of a rod with any mass per length. Bičák, Lynden-Bell, and Katz showed that it too arises as the metric of a counterrotating disc [bicak1993].

coordinates.name: Weyl

parameters.description: Dimensionless function of $\rho$ and $z$, with $-e^{2\psi}$ the norm of the Killing vector $\partial_t$ in the chart $x^0 = ct$; off the disc the spacetime is a vacuum exactly where $\partial_\rho^2\psi + \dfrac{1}{\rho}\partial_\rho\psi + \partial_z^2\psi = 0$, Laplace's equation in the flat space of $\rho$, $\phi$, and $z$, together with the equations for $\gamma$; for the disc of order $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ of Morgan and Morgan's family $c^2\psi$ is Newton's potential of a disc of mass $M$ and radius $a$ in the plane $z = 0$ with the surface density $\dfrac{(2n + 1)M}{2\pi a^2}\left(1 - \dfrac{\rho^2}{a^2}\right)^{n - 1/2}$, and for the first disc $\psi = -\dfrac{3m}{4a}\left(\left(1 + \eta^2 - \xi^2 + 3\xi^2\eta^2\right)\mathrm{arccot}\,\xi - \xi\left(3\eta^2 - 1\right)\right)$, where $m = GM/c^2$ and the oblate spheroidal coordinates $\xi \ge 0$ and $\eta$ are defined by $\rho = a\sqrt{\left(1 + \xi^2\right)\left(1 - \eta^2\right)}$ and $z = a\xi\eta$

Dimensionless function of $\rho$ and $z$ fixed by $\psi$ through $\partial_\rho\gamma = \rho\left(\left(\partial_\rho\psi\right)^2 - \left(\partial_z\psi\right)^2\right)$ and $\partial_z\gamma = 2\rho\,\partial_\rho\psi\,\partial_z\psi$, and zero on the axis $\rho = 0$, which is then free of conical singularities

coordinates.convention: We use Weyl's canonical coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ and $z$ lengths, and leave Weyl's two functions $\psi$ and $\gamma$ free. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Oblate Spheroidal

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass of the disc, measured at spatial infinity

Radius of the disc in Weyl's coordinates $\rho = a\sqrt{\left(1 + \xi^2\right)\left(1 - \eta^2\right)}$ and $z = a\xi\eta$, a length; the counter-rotating dust moves slower than light for $m/a < 2/(3\pi)$
The angle $\mathrm{arccot}\,\xi$, which falls from $\pi/2$ on the disc to zero at infinity

Weyl's first function for the first disc of Morgan and Morgan's family, with $c^2\psi$ Newton's potential of a disc of surface density $\dfrac{3M}{2\pi a^2}\sqrt{1 - \rho^2/a^2}$; it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_\xi\left(\left(1 + \xi^2\right)\partial_\xi\psi\right) + \partial_\eta\left(\left(1 - \eta^2\right)\partial_\eta\psi\right) = 0$, and on the disc $\psi = -\dfrac{3\pi m}{8a}\left(1 + \eta^2\right)$

Weyl's second function, fixed by $\psi$ through $\partial_\xi\gamma = \dfrac{1 - \eta^2}{\xi^2 + \eta^2}\left(\xi\left(1 + \xi^2\right)\left(\partial_\xi\psi\right)^2 - \xi\left(1 - \eta^2\right)\left(\partial_\eta\psi\right)^2 - 2\eta\left(1 + \xi^2\right)\partial_\xi\psi\,\partial_\eta\psi\right)$ and $\partial_\eta\gamma = \dfrac{1 + \xi^2}{\xi^2 + \eta^2}\left(\eta\left(1 + \xi^2\right)\left(\partial_\xi\psi\right)^2 - \eta\left(1 - \eta^2\right)\left(\partial_\eta\psi\right)^2 + 2\xi\left(1 - \eta^2\right)\partial_\xi\psi\,\partial_\eta\psi\right)$, and zero on the axis $\eta = \pm 1$

coordinates.convention: We use oblate spheroidal coordinates $(t, \xi, \eta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\xi$ and $\eta$ pure numbers, and write $\alpha$ for $\mathrm{arccot}\,\xi$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
